section_1.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Conditional Probability
section_1.content: Briefly review the definition of conditional probability P(A|B). Visualize this as 'zooming in' on the sample space of B to see how much of A overlaps within it.
section_1.example: Visualizing a Venn Diagram where the sample space S shrinks from the total area to just circle B.

section_2.title: The Definition of Independence
section_2.content: Explain that two events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A). This means the occurrence of B provides zero 'new' information about A.
section_2.example: Flipping a coin twice: The outcome of the first flip (Heads) does not change the probability of the second flip being Heads.

section_3.title: Introducing Bayes' Theorem: Updating Beliefs
section_3.content: Introduce the theorem as a bridge between P(A|B) and P(B|A). Explain it as a method for updating our initial belief (prior) based on new evidence (likelihood). Use a color-coded equation: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B).
section_3.example: A 'Robot Scout' identifying a target: If the robot sees a 'rustle in the bushes', how does it update the probability that a 'Fox' is present?

section_4.title: Synthesis: Bayes vs. Independence
section_4.content: Discuss what happens to Bayes' theorem if events are independent. Show that P(A|B) simplifies to P(A), effectively collapsing the complex theorem into a simple identity, illustrating why 'independence' is a special, simplified case.
section_4.example: Comparing a biased coin (dependent on the previous flip) versus a fair coin (independent of the previous flip) in a Bayesian update model.

section_5.title: Practical Application: The Diagnostic Test
section_5.content: Conclude with a real-world scenario to reinforce learning. Use a tree diagram to show the path of probabilities, highlighting the 'False Positive' trap.
section_5.example: A medical device (device A) testing for a rare virus. Calculate the probability of having the virus given a positive test result, emphasizing that the prior (low base rate) dominates the result.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)

section_1.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Conditional Probability
section_1.content: Briefly review the definition of conditional probability P(A|B). Visualize this as 'zooming in' on the sample space of B to see how much of A overlaps within it.
section_1.example: Visualizing a Venn Diagram where the sample space S shrinks from the total area to just circle B.

section_2.title: The Definition of Independence
section_2.content: Explain that two events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A). This means the occurrence of B provides zero 'new' information about A.
section_2.example: Flipping a coin twice: The outcome of the first flip (Heads) does not change the probability of the second flip being Heads.

section_3.title: Introducing Bayes' Theorem: Updating Beliefs
section_3.content: Introduce the theorem as a bridge between P(A|B) and P(B|A). Explain it as a method for updating our initial belief (prior) based on new evidence (likelihood). Use a color-coded equation: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B).
section_3.example: A 'Robot Scout' identifying a target: If the robot sees a 'rustle in the bushes', how does it update the probability that a 'Fox' is present?

section_4.title: Synthesis: Bayes vs. Independence
section_4.content: Discuss what happens to Bayes' theorem if events are independent. Show that P(A|B) simplifies to P(A), effectively collapsing the complex theorem into a simple identity, illustrating why 'independence' is a special, simplified case.
section_4.example: Comparing a biased coin (dependent on the previous flip) versus a fair coin (independent of the previous flip) in a Bayesian update model.

section_5.title: Practical Application: The Diagnostic Test
section_5.content: Conclude with a real-world scenario to reinforce learning. Use a tree diagram to show the path of probabilities, highlighting the 'False Positive' trap.
section_5.example: A medical device (device A) testing for a rare virus. Calculate the probability of having the virus given a positive test result, emphasizing that the prior (low base rate) dominates the result.
